### `.github/workflows/always-broken.yml`
````text
000001 | name: Always Broken (CI fixture)
000002 | [blank]
000003 | # Standing "always broken" CI fixture for testing `prash fix --ci` and
000004 | # `prash investigate <repo> --ci` without needing a fresh push each time.
000005 | # This workflow ONLY runs when something is pushed to the `prash-broken-ci`
000006 | # branch -- it deliberately does NOT run on main or on pull requests, so it
000007 | # never affects the real CI signal. The job always fails (exit 1) after
000008 | # producing a realistic-looking error, giving the diagnosis brain a stable,
000009 | # re-runnable failing run to chew on.
000010 | #
000011 | # To use the fixture:
000012 | #   prash fix <owner>/<repo> --ci --run-id <run-id> --noninteractive
000013 | #   prash investigate <owner>/<repo> --ci
000014 | #
000015 | # To trigger a fresh failure without touching main, push any commit to this
000016 | # branch (an empty commit works): git commit --allow-empty -m "re-trigger"
000017 | [blank]
000018 | on:
000019 |   push:
000020 |     branches: [prash-broken-ci]
000021 | [blank]
000022 | jobs:
000023 |   always-broken:
000024 |     runs-on: ubuntu-latest
000025 |     steps:
000026 |       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
000027 | [blank]
000028 |       - name: Simulate a broken step
000029 |         shell: bash
000030 |         run: |
000031 |           echo "::error::intentional fixture failure on prash-broken-ci"
000032 |           echo "flaky-network-error: connection reset by peer"
000033 |           echo "Traceback (most recent call last):"
000034 |           echo "  File \"app/deploy.py\", line 42, in deploy"
000035 |           echo "    raise DeploymentError(\"upstream service unavailable\")"
000036 |           exit 1
````

````text
000001 | name: CI
000002 | [blank]

000004 |   push:
000005 |     branches: [main]

000007 | [blank]
000008 | jobs:
000009 |   test:
000010 |     # Both matter: Aryan develops on Windows, Aradhya on macOS, and Prash v2
000011 |     # is a CLI tool — path handling and shell behaviour differ between them.
000012 |     # Catching that here is cheaper than catching it when one of you can't
000013 |     # run the other's code.
000014 |     strategy:
000015 |       fail-fast: false
000016 |       matrix:
000017 |         os: [ubuntu-latest, windows-latest, macos-latest]
000018 |     runs-on: ${{ matrix.os }}
000019 | [blank]
000020 |     steps:
000021 |       - uses: actions/checkout@v4
000022 | [blank]
000023 |       - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
000024 |         with:
000025 |           python-version: '3.12'
000026 | [blank]
000027 |       - name: Install dependencies
000028 |         shell: bash
000029 |         # Written before pyproject.toml existed (repo was docs-only scaffolding
000030 |         # at the time) -- this originally only handled requirements.txt, so it
000031 |         # never actually installed the `prash` package itself. Once real code
000032 |         # landed with imports like `from prash.actions...`, every test failed
000033 |         # with ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'prash'. `pip install -e .`
000034 |         # is what was missing. Keep the requirements.txt fallback too, in case
000035 |         # anyone adds one instead of extending pyproject.toml later.
000036 |         run: |
000037 |           python -m pip install --upgrade pip
000038 |           if [ -f pyproject.toml ]; then pip install -e ".[dev]"; fi
000039 |           if [ -f requirements.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements.txt; fi
000040 |           if [ -f requirements-dev.txt ]; then pip install -r requirements-dev.txt; fi
000041 |           pip install ruff
000042 | [blank]
000043 |       - name: Lint
000044 |         shell: bash
000045 |         run: ruff check . || echo "::warning::ruff reported issues (not failing the build yet)"
000046 | [blank]
000047 |       - name: Tests
000048 |         shell: bash
000049 |         # Exit code 5 = "no tests collected", which is fine while the repo is
000050 |         # still being scaffolded. Any real test failure still fails the build.
000051 |         #
000052 |         # `set +e` is required: GitHub runs this step under `bash -e`, which
000053 |         # aborts on the first non-zero exit — so without it, pytest's exit 5
000054 |         # kills the script before the check below can run.
000055 |         run: |
000056 |           set +e
000057 |           pytest -q
000058 |           code=$?
000059 |           set -e
000060 |           if [ "$code" -eq 5 ]; then
000061 |             echo "No tests collected yet — passing."
000062 |             exit 0
000063 |           fi
000064 |           exit "$code"
000065 | [blank]

000052 | ## 4. The interface — reconciled with the code that already exists
000053 | [blank]
000054 | **Read this before proposing signatures.** Lear already has a clean two-layer architecture. The rewrite extends it; it does **not** invent a parallel one.
000055 | [blank]
000056 | - **Read/state layer — `prash/connectors/`.** Base class `Connector` in `connectors/base.py` (abstract `authenticate()`, `locate()`, plus `fetch_logs()`, `poll_state() -> ResourceState`, and `read_capabilities`/`write_capabilities` metadata). Every connector is a class `XConnector(Connector)` — **except `kubernetes.py`, which is module-level functions and is the odd one out** (see M1).
000057 | - **Write layer — `prash/actions/`.** Every write is already a discrete `Action` subclass with an `ActionSpec(id, summary, risk_tier, reversible, capabilities, approval_hint)`, dispatched through `prash/dispatch.py` against `prash/permissions.py`. Real examples in the tree today: `datadog_mute` (SAFE), `grafana_silence` (SAFE), `restart_pod` (SAFE), `rollback` (APPROVAL), `scale` (APPROVAL), `pagerduty_incident`, `execute_aws/gcp/azure`, `vercel_deploy`, `snyk_ignore`, `gitleaks_escalate`, `open_pr`.
000058 | [blank]
000059 | So the three new capabilities land in **two different layers**, not one:
000060 | [blank]
000061 | ### 4a. `watch()` and `get_stats()` → read layer, on the `Connector` ABC
000062 | [blank]
000063 | Added to `connectors/base.py` as concrete-default methods (raising `NotImplementedError`, same as `fetch_logs`/`poll_state` do today), then implemented per connector:
000064 | [blank]
000065 | ```python
000066 | def watch(self, target: str) -> "WatchHandle":
000067 |     """Begin monitoring `target`; the handle feeds the shared watcher loop (§4c)."""
000068 | [blank]
000069 | def get_stats(self, target: str, since: datetime | None = None) -> list["ConnectorEvent"]:
000070 |     """Return a time series of normalized events for `target`, optionally since a time."""
000071 | ```
000072 | [blank]
000073 | **Reconciliation with existing methods — do not duplicate them:**
000074 | - `poll_state() -> ResourceState` stays as-is: the *point-in-time* health check ("what is the state right now").
000075 | - `get_stats()` is the *time series* ("what happened, on a shared clock"). It may call `poll_state()`/`fetch_logs()` internally; it does not replace them.
000076 | - `ResourceState`/`ConnectorState` (existing) describe current health; `ConnectorEvent` (new, below) is the cross-provider timeline row. Both coexist.
000077 | [blank]
000078 | ### 4b. `alert()` → write layer, a new gated `Action` per provider (NOT a loose method)
000079 | [blank]
000080 | Pushing an outbound alert is a side-effecting write. It must go through the same path as every other write — an `Action` with a risk tier — or it bypasses Lear's core human-approval USP. Concretely, one new action per provider that can alert (e.g. `datadog_alert`, `pagerduty_page`), each:
000081 | [blank]
000082 | ```python
000083 | class PagerDutyPageAction(Action):
000084 |     spec = ActionSpec(
000085 |         id="pagerduty-page",
000086 |         summary="Page an on-call responder via PagerDuty",
000087 |         risk_tier=RiskTier.APPROVAL,   # outbound + not cleanly reversible → always asks
000088 |         reversible=False,
000089 |         capabilities=("alert",),
000090 |     )
000091 | ```
000092 | [blank]
000093 | Default tier for outbound alerts is **APPROVAL** (always prompts, even in bypass mode). A provider whose "alert" is genuinely reversible and internal-only may argue SAFE at M0 — decided per provider, in code, with the reasoning logged.
000094 | [blank]

000098 | class ConnectorEvent(TypedDict):

000100 |     connector: str        # e.g. "datadog", "kubernetes", "github"
000101 |     event_type: str       # e.g. "metric_spike", "pod_crash", "deploy", "ci_failure"
000102 |     summary: str          # one human-readable line — what the diagnosis brain reads first
000103 |     raw: dict             # untouched provider-specific payload, for drill-down
000104 | ```

000171 | | 2026-09-07 | G0 (Aradhya) | GitHub Actions CI connector — API-scope audit + alert-tier decision (no code) | **Auth:** existing `GITHUB_TOKEN` (classic or fine-grained PAT), `Bearer` header, stdlib `urllib` — no new credentials. **watch()/get_stats():** both read `GET /repos/{repo}/actions/runs` (the existing `workflow_runs()` method; `_run_state()` already maps status/conclusion → `ConnectorState`). Scope: public repos need only a token; private repos need `actions:read` (fine-grained) or `repo` (classic). `get_stats(repo, since)` = recent runs as a `ConnectorEvent` timeline (event_type `ci_failure`/`ci_success`/`ci_in_progress`); `watch()` = `WatchHandle.poll()` model, dedup by run-id + conclusion (mirrors PagerDuty's id+status dedup), emitting an event only when a run newly completes as a failure. **alert() decision: `github-open-issue`, risk_tier=APPROVAL, reversible=True.** Rationale (matches long-term vision): the primary CI value is already the `open-pr`/`apply-ci-fix` fix→PR flow, so the alert slot is the *escalation* path — when Lear has a diagnosis but no safe auto-fix, it files an issue carrying that diagnosis as a durable, team-visible record (`POST /repos/{repo}/issues`, needs `issues:write` fine-grained or `repo` classic). Direct CI analog of `pagerduty-page`/`datadog-alert` (outbound + team-visible → APPROVAL); reversible=True because an issue can be closed, unlike a page. Rejected: *skip-like-k8s* (nothing external watches CI failures the way Datadog/PagerDuty watch k8s, so CI needs its own escalation artifact) and *rerun-workflow-as-alert* (`re_run_job()` already exists as a capability; re-running is remediation, not alert — belongs in the fix layer later, not the alert slot). **Code note for G1:** `_request()` has no rate-limit handling; a watch loop should honor 429 + `Retry-After`/`X-RateLimit-Reset` like the Datadog/PagerDuty connectors do. |

000188 | | 2026-09-07 | Aradhya (agent-assisted) | **Datadog M4 loop live-verified end-to-end** — the credentials-gated §5b checklist pass ran against the real org, and four real bugs fell out of it (all fixed same day, each with a regression test): (1) **`get_stats()` missed every monitor-alert event**: the Events v2 query used a bare `monitor_id:<id>` facet — matches ZERO events; monitor-alert events live in the events pipeline where facets need the log-style `@` prefix, and they nest title/source/transition under `attributes.attributes` (with epoch-ms timestamps). The monitor had just triggered and recovered on camera, both events were in the stream, and the old query still returned 0. `_monitor_events` now queries `@monitor_id:<id>`, parses the nested shape (flat shape kept as fallback), and surfaces `monitor.transition` (source_state→destination_state) in `raw` for the brain. (2) **`datadog-alert` couldn't post at all**: this org's API key is **denied Events v2 intake** (403 with both keys, 401 API-only) while the legacy v1 intake accepts the same key — the M2 scope-audit row above said "no new credentials required", which is true for reads but wrong for v2 intake under this org's key permissions. `post_event` now falls back to v1 intake on permission-shaped 401/403 (same event stream, `via` marker names what landed; other errors still propagate), and `get_event` falls back to v1 on 404 so verification works for v1-posted events. (3) **`verify()` raced Datadog's intake→searchability propagation**: a just-posted event 404s on GET for a few seconds, and v2 GET returns its own encoded `data.id` (original id nested at `attributes.attributes.evt.id`), so the old strict id-compare failed even when the event existed. Verify now retries bounded (2s/4s), accepts both id shapes, and still reports honestly ("may still be propagating") if it never confirms. (4) **Desktop toast silently broken on Windows for long notifications** (hit by the Datadog watch, latent for every loop): plyer's win32 balloon backend packs title/message into NOTIFYICONDATAW struct fields capped at 64 chars, and the ValueError fires in its worker thread AFTER notify() returned True — the caller can neither catch it nor know the toast never showed. `watcher._toast_clamp` bounds both strings; console and team channels keep the full text. Also wired `--text/--priority/--tags` on `prash run` (the `datadog-alert` action read them from ctx.extra but no CLI flag populated them — the documented checklist command was unrunnable) and fixed the action's "priority None" plan text. **Live loop proven**: heal → baseline silent → trip → Alert notified in one poll cycle → 8 Alert polls deduped → heal → recovery notified → investigate/stats timeline shows all [Triggered]/[Recovered] events → APPROVAL prompt + decline path → grant path posts + verifies + audits → mute (auto-safe) verified → no-targets error (exit 2) + `DATADOG_WATCH_MONITORS` path. **Only §5b's brain row remains blocked**: no valid LLM key on this machine (test.env's DEEPSEEK key is an invalid placeholder, KIMI empty) — needs one real DEEPSEEK_API_KEY/KIMI_API_KEY in local .env; the code path is unit- + eval-covered. Suite green (see §3 for the still-open live false-positive measurement, which this pass unblocked the data for but which still needs the LLM pass). |

000001 | # Lear / Prash Application Audit Report

000012 | [blank]
000013 | ## 1. Executive summary
000014 | [blank]
000015 | Lear is a local-first AI DevOps/SRE application with two principal faces:
000016 | [blank]
000017 | 1. **Desktop console:** React 19 + TypeScript + Vite, intended to run inside a Tauri 2 shell but also usable as a browser/Vite page. It talks to a local FastAPI bridge with relative `/api/...` URLs for HTTP. It provides onboarding, integrations, projects/stacks, service telemetry widgets, watch controls, dashboard activity, notifications, settings, chat, and incident-related chat surfaces.
000018 | 2. **Python agent/server surfaces:** the `prash` package provides a CLI/TUI/REPL, a FastAPI desktop bridge, 13 provider connectors, a permissioned action dispatcher, diagnosis and remediation flows, a watcher, local memory, incidents, email/Slack integration, and several FastAPI-served HTML/demo pages.
000019 | [blank]
000020 | The core trust model is local credentials plus local file persistence. There is **no SQL database, ORM, migration layer, or hosted persistence implementation in this repository**. Configuration and runtime state are split across `.env`, `prash.yaml`, `.prash/*.json`, `.prash/audit.log`, generated email HTML, process memory, browser localStorage, and external provider state.
000021 | [blank]
000022 | The main operational pipeline is:
000023 | [blank]
000024 | ```text
000025 | Desktop / CLI / chat / incident ingress
000026 |         ↓
000027 | connector registry or intent resolver
000028 |         ↓
000029 | provider read surface or action dispatcher
000030 |         ↓
000031 | plan → circuit breaker → permission decision → approval/secret → execute
000032 |         ↓
000033 | verify → audit → local activity/notification → UI/WebSocket
000034 | ```
000035 | [blank]
000036 | The repository has a substantial implementation, but the current code and roadmap make clear that it is not yet production-hardened. Confirmed high-impact observations include:
000037 | [blank]
000038 | - FastAPI CORS is permissive: `allow_origins=["*"]` with credentials enabled.
000039 | - `/ws/events` accepts connections without authentication.
000040 | - API routes generally have no user/session authentication or CSRF protection; incident approval endpoints accept both GET and POST.
000041 | - The desktop and server use multiple independent WebSocket consumers, each opening `ws://127.0.0.1:8000/ws/events`.
000042 | - The frontend’s `LearContext` looks for `c.configured`, while the registry serialization returns `status`, so the context-level configured count can remain zero even when integrations are configured.
000043 | - The Tauri Rust shell only exposes the template `greet` command; it does not own backend lifecycle, credentials, or native functionality.
000044 | - The Vite proxy, frontend WebSocket default, npm root server script, and launchers assume loopback addresses, which is incompatible with a browser-facing sandbox/live-preview deployment without configuration changes.
000045 | - Demo/incident/channel code contains fixed infrastructure narrative, localhost URLs, default recipient addresses, and synthetic-looking telemetry text even though the desktop bridge advertises dynamic/no-hardcoded data.
000046 | - `server.py` is approximately 3,895 lines and `cli.py` approximately 1,360 lines; the roadmap explicitly marks decomposition and state extraction as not started.
000047 | - The environment used for this audit had no `pytest` executable and no `desktop/node_modules`; Python compilation passed, but backend tests and frontend build/tests could not run.

000156 | ## 3. Application surfaces and startup
000157 | [blank]
000158 | ### 3.1 Browser/Tauri desktop startup
000159 | [blank]
000160 | 1. Vite serves the React app at port 1420. The Tauri config points at `http://localhost:1420` in development and `../dist` for packaged frontend output.
000161 | 2. `main.tsx` renders `App`.
000162 | 3. `App.tsx` calls `GET /api/config` once during startup.
000163 | 4. If no configured services are returned, the app renders `Wizard` as an onboarding gate.
000164 | 5. Otherwise it renders the sidebar and the selected main surface, with the global Copilot/chat drawer and toast layer.
000165 | 6. URL query parameters can select a tab or open chat. The default context tab is `dashboard`.
000166 | 7. `LearContext` loads system version, connectors, projects, and active watches, then maintains active project/environment, watcher state, chat state, notification count, and toast state.
000167 | 8. Project and environment choices are browser-local only under `lear_active_project_id` and `lear_active_environment`.
000168 | [blank]
000169 | ### 3.2 Python server startup
000170 | [blank]
000171 | `prash.server`:
000172 | [blank]
000173 | - Loads root `.env` with `dotenv.load_dotenv(..., override=True)` at import time.
000174 | - Uses root-relative `ENV_PATH`, `YAML_PATH`, and `.prash/notifications.json` paths.
000175 | - Creates a FastAPI app with a lifespan handler.
000176 | - On lifespan start, restores watches from `prash.yaml`, loads notifications, starts the WebSocket polling task, starts the connector health-check task, and attempts to start the IMAP listener.
000177 | - On shutdown, cancels tasks, stops the IMAP listener, stops watch handles, and clears in-memory watch structures.
000178 | - Keeps watches, WebSocket clients, activity, notifications, connection states, and dashboard cache in module-level mutable globals.
000179 | [blank]
000180 | ### 3.3 CLI startup
000181 | [blank]
000182 | `prash.cli:main` loads local credentials, exports relevant cluster environment variables, builds the dispatcher, and routes commands through the permission/audit/circuit path. The CLI can run as one-shot commands, a Textual TUI, or a persistent REPL. The action dispatcher itself is shared conceptually with server chat execution, but the FastAPI chat executor invokes CLI parsing in-process.
000183 | [blank]
000184 | ---
000185 | [blank]
000186 | ## 4. Desktop UI: what users see and how it operates
000187 | [blank]
000188 | ### 4.1 Navigation
000189 | [blank]
000190 | The sidebar exposes Dashboard, Lear Chat, Projects, Integrations, Activity Log, Notifications, and Settings. The app also displays connection/watcher indicators, active project and environment controls, the app version, and a global Copilot affordance.
000191 | [blank]
000192 | ### 4.2 Wizard
000193 | [blank]
000194 | The onboarding wizard fetches registry metadata, presents integration selection and credential/location/notification steps, posts configuration, and can auto-import configured services into the default project. It is shown whenever `/api/config` reports no configured services.
000195 | [blank]
000196 | ### 4.3 Dashboard
000197 | [blank]
000198 | `Dashboard.tsx` fetches `/api/dashboard/summary`, `/api/dashboard/activity`, and `/api/incidents`. It presents an aggregate health score, service counts, active watches, recent activity, connected service cards, incident status, quick actions, and provider-specific explanatory content. Service cards route into telemetry or Copilot. The dashboard uses dynamic API results but still contains provider-specific presentation branches and hardcoded wording that should be treated separately from live metrics.
000199 | [blank]
000200 | ### 4.4 Integrations
000201 | [blank]
000202 | `Integrations.tsx`:
000203 | [blank]
000204 | - Fetches `/api/connectors`.
000205 | - Filters/searches the registry by category and configured/unconfigured state.
000206 | - Expands `ConnectorForm` inline.
000207 | - Calls `/validate` for a manual health check.
000208 | - Calls `/disconnect` after an inline confirmation.
000209 | - Displays masked metadata, identity, last verification, docs, and transient success/error messages.
000210 | [blank]
000211 | `ConnectorForm.tsx` renders the registry-provided auth field schema, including text/password/file/select/textarea styles, submits to `/api/connectors/{id}/connect`, preserves existing values where supported, and never intentionally displays raw credential values.
000212 | [blank]
000213 | ### 4.5 Projects and stacks
000214 | [blank]
000215 | Projects are YAML-backed objects with:
000216 | [blank]
000217 | ```text
000218 | project = {
000219 |   id, name, created_at,
000220 |   environments: [
000221 |     { name, services: [
000222 |       { connector_id, resource_id?, display_name? }
000223 |     ] }
000224 |   ]
000225 | }
000226 | ```
000227 | [blank]
000228 | `Projects.tsx` lists projects, auto-imports configured connectors, opens a four-step create modal, deletes projects, and opens details. `ProjectCreate.tsx` creates project identity, environments, attached services, and posts `/api/projects`. `ProjectDetail.tsx`:
000229 | [blank]
000230 | - polls `/api/projects/{id}/status` immediately and every 20 seconds;
000231 | - switches environments;
000232 | - adds/removes services and environments with `PUT`;
000233 | - discovers real resources from `/api/connectors/{id}/resources`;
000234 | - routes a service to Dashboard telemetry or service-scoped Copilot.
000235 | [blank]
000236 | ### 4.6 Telemetry widgets
000237 | [blank]
000238 | `ServiceWidget.tsx` loads connector metadata, metrics, status, widgets, and active watches. It can configure/reset widget layouts, display six widget families (gauge, line chart, bar chart, metric card, event timeline, status grid), start/stop watches, and provide connector-specific action affordances. `WidgetConfigurator.tsx` calls `/generate-widgets` and can save results. The server stores custom layouts under `widgets.{connector_id}.{resource_id-or-default}` in `prash.yaml`.
000239 | [blank]
000240 | Generation is:
000241 | [blank]
000242 | ```text
000243 | live connector state/stats + registry templates + user prompt
000244 |         ↓
000245 | LLM JSON generation when an AI key exists
000246 |         ↓
000247 | JSON extraction/validation/layout normalization
000248 |         ↓
000249 | deterministic template/metric fallback when unavailable
000250 |         ↓
000251 | optional YAML persistence
000252 | ```
000253 | [blank]
000254 | ### 4.7 Watcher panel and live state
000255 | [blank]
000256 | `WatcherPanel.tsx`, `useWatcher.ts`, `LearContext`, `useNotifications`, and service widgets each consume the watch API/WebSocket surfaces. They maintain overlapping local views of active watches/events. Backend events are JSON payloads with `watch_id`, `connector`, `event_type`, `summary`, `raw`, and `timestamp`.
000257 | [blank]
000258 | The frontend WebSocket default is hardcoded to `ws://127.0.0.1:8000/ws/events`. Multiple `useWebSocket()` instances open separate sockets rather than sharing a single provider. This is a concrete duplication and deployment concern.
000259 | [blank]
000260 | ### 4.8 Activity and notifications
000261 | [blank]
000262 | `ActivityLog.tsx` queries `/api/activity` and supports text, connector, type, severity, time-range, and pagination views. It combines live in-memory events and disk audit entries. `Notifications.tsx` queries the persistent notification queue, marks individual/all items read, clears the queue, and routes relevant notifications to Dashboard, Settings, or chat. `NotificationToast.tsx` renders transient toasts from the context queue.
000263 | [blank]
000264 | ### 4.9 Chat and Copilot
000265 | [blank]
000266 | There are two desktop chat experiences:
000267 | [blank]
000268 | - `Chatbot.tsx` — global/service-scoped drawer, greeting, message stream, incident context, email/Slack controls, and action execution.
000269 | - `ChatWorkspace.tsx` — persistent session workspace with origin filters for dashboard, Slack, email, and incidents.
000270 | [blank]
000271 | Chat can use direct telemetry-driven SRE analysis, fast intent resolution, async LLM intent fallback, SSE streaming, persistent sessions, incident chat, and action execution. A user click on “Execute Action” is treated by the server as the approval and temporarily replaces CLI’s interactive ask implementation with an always-true `_ChatUiApprovedAsk` for that request.
000272 | [blank]
000273 | ### 4.10 Settings
000274 | [blank]
000275 | `Settings.tsx` fetches `/api/settings`, `/api/config`, and `/api/system/version`. It edits model, permission mode, poll interval, retention days, desktop notifications, degraded alerts, Slack, Discord, and PagerDuty settings. The server persists settings into both `prash.yaml` and selected `.env` keys.

000391 | ## 6. Connector matrix
000392 | [blank]
000393 | All connectors inherit the conceptual contract in `connectors/base.py`: `authenticate`, `locate`, optional `fetch_logs`, `poll_state`, `watch`, and `get_stats`. Every event is normalized as timestamp, connector, event type, summary, and provider-specific raw payload.
000394 | [blank]
000395 | | ID | Provider/category | Registry auth fields | Registry flags | Read/write behavior |
000396 | |---|---|---|---|---|
000397 | | `aws` | AWS EC2 / infrastructure | `AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID` required; `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` required; `AWS_REGION` optional | watch, stats, execute | STS/EC2 auth; instance locate/state; CloudWatch/log reads; watch/stats; EC2 command execution via action |
000398 | | `azure` | Microsoft Azure / infrastructure | subscription, tenant, client ID, client secret required; location optional | watch, stats, execute | Azure identity/VM state/log reads; VM command execution |
000399 | | `gcp` | Google Cloud / infrastructure | `GCP_PROJECT_ID` required; service-account file optional; region optional | watch, stats, execute | Compute/Cloud Monitoring reads and watch; GCE command execution |
000400 | | `kubernetes` | Kubernetes / infrastructure | kubeconfig/context/namespace all optional | watch, stats, execute | pod locate/status/logs/events/stats/watch; restart, scale, exec, ConfigMap/Secret edit, rollback/apply actions |
000401 | | `vercel` | Vercel / infrastructure | `VERCEL_TOKEN` required; team optional | watch, stats, execute | deployment locate/log/state/watch/stats; redeploy and rollback |
000402 | | `github` | GitHub Actions / CI/CD | `GITHUB_TOKEN` required; repo optional | watch, stats, execute false | workflow/repo/check-run/log reads; watch/stats; PR/issue/re-run/apply-fix actions |
000403 | | `gitlab` | GitLab CI / CI/CD | `GITLAB_TOKEN` required; base URL optional | watch, stats, execute false | pipeline/project/job trace reads; watch/stats; MR/issue/apply-fix actions |
000404 | | `datadog` | Datadog / monitoring | API key + app key required; site optional | watch, stats, execute true | monitor state/log/event/stats/watch; mute monitor and alert actions |
000405 | | `grafana` | Grafana / monitoring | URL + API key required | watch, stats, execute true | alert rule/annotation state/stats/watch; silence action |
000406 | | `pagerduty` | PagerDuty / monitoring | REST API key required; from-email/routing-key optional | watch, stats, execute true | incident/on-call/dependency state/stats/watch; acknowledge, resolve, trigger/page actions |
000407 | | `snyk` | Snyk / security | API token + org ID required | watch, stats, execute true | project vulnerability state; bounded ignore action |
000408 | | `gitleaks` | local Gitleaks / security | binary path optional | watch, stats, execute false | local executable scan, state/log-like results; never includes secret text; escalation action can page PagerDuty |
000409 | | `terraform` | Terraform / IaC | state path/use-cloud/API token all optional | watch, stats, execute true | local state/drift reads and watch; init/apply actions |
000410 | [blank]
000411 | ### Connector lifecycle details
000412 | [blank]
000413 | - Registry instances are lazily constructed and cached by connector ID.
000414 | - `/validate` explicitly clears a connector cache before checking because provider auth state may otherwise remain stale.
000415 | - Server connection state is cached in `_connection_states`; the cache tracks `status`, `last_verified`, `last_checked`, `error`, and `identity`.
000416 | - `.env` is treated as the root server credential store. The CLI’s `CredentialStore` can fall back to `~/.prash/.env`, but the FastAPI bridge uses its root-relative `.env` path.
000417 | - Resource discovery is not uniform: the server has explicit discovery logic for AWS, Kubernetes, GitHub, Vercel, and Datadog; other registered connectors can return an empty resource list even when configured.
000418 | - Provider APIs and local subprocesses are not exercised in this audit because that would require credentials and could mutate external systems.
000419 | [blank]

000421 | [blank]
000422 | ## 7. Action, permission, and safety matrix
000423 | [blank]
000424 | ### 7.1 Dispatcher contract
000425 | [blank]
000426 | `Dispatcher.run()` performs:
000427 | [blank]
000428 | 1. Resolve registered action.
000429 | 2. Build a side-effect-free `Plan`.
000430 | 3. Check `CircuitBreaker.is_open(resource)`.
000431 | 4. Call `permissions.decide(mode, risk_tier, environment, grant)`.
000432 | 5. Refuse or prompt as required.
000433 | 6. Execute.
000434 | 7. If successful, call `verify`.
000435 | 8. Record actual execution in the breaker.
000436 | 9. Append an audit record for refusal, skip, success, failure, or input-needed results.
000437 | [blank]
000438 | `--dry-run` calls `action.dry_run()` and never executes. The dispatcher now reports refusal honestly in read-only dry runs.
000439 | [blank]
000440 | ### 7.2 Permission modes
000441 | [blank]
000442 | - `read-only` — refuses all writes.
000443 | - `ask` — prompts for safe and approval actions.
000444 | - `auto-safe` — allows `SAFE`; prompts `APPROVAL`.
000445 | - `environment-scoped` — allows `SAFE` outside `production`; prompts in production.
000446 | - `bypass` — allows `SAFE`; still prompts approval-tier actions; never overrides `NEVER`.
000447 | [blank]
000448 | `NEVER` always refuses. The current registered action set does not visibly include a `NEVER` action, but the engine supports the tier.
000449 | [blank]
000450 | ### 7.3 Registered actions
000451 | [blank]
000452 | | Action IDs | Tier | Reversible / side effect summary |
000453 | |---|---|---|
000454 | | `open-pr`, `apply-ci-fix`, `apply-manifest-fix`, `apply-gitlab-ci-fix`, `request-secret`, `restart-pod`, `datadog-mute-monitor`, `grafana-silence-alert`, `terraform-init`, `vercel-redeploy` | SAFE | Writes PR/MR or local secret, restarts/silences/mutes, initializes Terraform, or redeploys; several are marked reversible, but “SAFE” means permission behavior, not no side effect |
000455 | | `pagerduty-acknowledge` | SAFE | Changes incident acknowledgement; marked non-reversible in its spec |
000456 | | `rollback`, `scale`, `edit-configmap`, `edit-secret`, `exec`, `execute-aws`, `execute-gcp`, `execute-azure`, `pagerduty-resolve`, `pagerduty-page`, `vercel-rollback`, `datadog-alert`, `aws-alert`, `gcp-alert`, `github-open-issue`, `gitlab-open-issue`, `snyk-ignore-issue`, `terraform-apply` | APPROVAL | External writes, execution, paging, issue creation, secret/config changes, or infrastructure apply |
000457 | | `gitleaks-escalate` | SAFE in its spec | Runs local scan and can create a PagerDuty incident; marked non-reversible despite external escalation |
000458 | [blank]
000459 | `edit-secret` explicitly avoids printing values; Gitleaks tests assert leaked secret text does not reach state/log output. The full exact specs are in the individual action modules and `tests/test_actions.py`.
000460 | [blank]
000461 | ### 7.4 Circuit breaker
000462 | [blank]
000463 | Default: five actions per resource in 60 seconds, persisted at `.prash/circuit.json`, configurable via `PRASH_CIRCUIT_MAX_ACTIONS`, `PRASH_CIRCUIT_WINDOW_SECONDS`, and `PRASH_CIRCUIT_STATE_PATH`. Reset is explicit through `prash circuit reset`. The breaker is resource-keyed, not a full provider/account-wide safety budget.
000464 | [blank]
000465 | ### 7.5 Audit record
000466 | [blank]
000467 | `AuditLog.append()` writes JSON lines to `.prash/audit.log` with:
000468 | [blank]
000469 | ```text
000470 | id, ts, seq, action, risk_tier, mode, decision, environment, actor,
000471 | status, summary, verification_ok, extra
000472 | ```
000473 | [blank]
000474 | It is append-only by API design and used by `/api/activity` and `prash audit`. Chat execution also appends a separate audit-shaped record with actor `chat_copilot`, meaning a single chat-triggered action can have both dispatcher and chat-level records.

000478 | ## 8. AI, diagnosis, and remediation flow
000479 | [blank]
000480 | ### 8.1 Model clients
000481 | [blank]
000482 | `prash/brain/kimi_client.py` uses lazy AsyncOpenAI clients for DeepSeek and Kimi. It reads API keys/models from environment, recreates clients when the running event loop changes, supports structured tool calls, JSON extraction, recoverable/transient error handling, retries, and provider fallback. No model call log is persisted to a hosted database; it is logged locally.
000483 | [blank]
000484 | `.env.example` also lists Gemini, while current active chat/diagnosis paths emphasize DeepSeek/Kimi/OpenAI-compatible clients. The settings UI advertises additional models that are not all wired to distinct client implementations.
000485 | [blank]
000486 | ### 8.2 Diagnosis schema
000487 | [blank]
000488 | `Diagnosis` includes problem summary, root cause, fix description, fix type, confidence, flaky flag, file changes, category, truncation warning, speculative flag, required secrets, recommended runtime/monitoring action, ConfigMap patch, and ranked options.
000489 | [blank]
000490 | `FileChange` enforces either exact/whitespace-tolerant unique edits against existing content or complete new content for genuinely new files. It rejects unsafe paths and oversized content. `Diagnosis` coerces inconsistent fix types and derives `recommended_action` from a default option when an options menu is used.
000491 | [blank]
000492 | ### 8.3 CI diagnosis
000493 | [blank]
000494 | 1. GitHub/GitLab connector fetches workflow/pipeline logs.
000495 | 2. Log fetchers cap ZIP/extracted/log sizes, prioritize failing jobs, filter error lines with context, preserve matrix summaries, and avoid phantom raw-tail sections for multi-failure splitting.
000496 | 3. `multi_diagnosis.py` splits independent job sections and diagnoses them concurrently with a configurable cap (`PRASH_MAX_DIAGNOSIS_CONCURRENCY`, default 3).
000497 | 4. Partial results are represented as “diagnosed X of N,” not falsely “fixed.”
000498 | 5. GitHub diagnosis grounds proposed edits against real repository contents and can attempt edit repair.
000499 | 6. CLI rendering presents diagnoses/options; applying CI/manifest fixes runs through action dispatch and can reconcile a new branch CI run with bounded attempts and error signatures.
000500 | [blank]
000501 | ### 8.4 Runtime/monitoring diagnosis
000502 | [blank]
000503 | `fix.py` gathers provider context from Kubernetes, AWS, GCP, Datadog, PagerDuty, or Grafana and calls the same diagnosis brain. Automatic mapping currently includes:
000504 | [blank]
000505 | ```text
000506 | restart_pod          → restart-pod
000507 | edit_configmap       → edit-configmap
000508 | action mute_monitor  → datadog-mute-monitor
000509 | acknowledge_incident → pagerduty-acknowledge
000510 | silence_alert        → grafana-silence-alert
000511 | ```
000512 | [blank]
000513 | Rollback and scale are recognized by the schema but are intentionally not always auto-dispatched through the runtime seam. The diagnosis prompt distinguishes transient/wedged pods from deterministic broken image/config/command cases and allows an explicit no-action escalation or ranked options.
000514 | [blank]
000515 | ### 8.5 Correlation and memory
000516 | [blank]
000517 | - `correlation.py` clusters normalized events by a two-minute running-gap window, records distinct connectors, and formats multi-source context.
000518 | - `local_memory.py` stores verified fixes, repeated error signatures, category outcomes, known-good files, flaky tests, and dependency patterns in `.prash/memory.json` (or `PRASH_MEMORY_PATH`).
000519 | - `repo_memory.py` is only a local dataclass/prompt renderer. The old Supabase-backed builder was intentionally removed.
000520 | - `save_fix()` is called from fix flows after verification to learn from outcomes.
000521 | [blank]
000522 | ### 8.6 Confirmed model/brain caveats
000523 | [blank]
000524 | - `diagnosis_agent.py` has a historical docstring describing itself as CI-shaped/unchanged even though the file and schema now include runtime/monitoring context paths; documentation is stale.
000525 | - Some server Copilot paths contain highly specific production assumptions about AWS EKS, `lear-demo`, `ap-south-1`, checkout services, and expected CPU ranges. These should not be treated as generic live telemetry behavior.
000526 | - Chat fallback strings claim stable AWS/Kubernetes telemetry even when model/provider calls fail; this is a product honesty concern distinct from the connector metrics API.
000527 | [blank]

000530 | ## 9. Watcher and notification architecture
000531 | [blank]
000532 | ### 9.1 CLI watcher
000533 | [blank]
000534 | `prash watcher.py` supports:
000535 | [blank]
000536 | - Kubernetes pod problem transitions (`CrashLoopBackOff`, `OOMKilled`, `ImagePullBackOff`, stuck-pending) with deduped notifications.
000537 | - Terraform state/drift polling.
000538 | - Shared connector watch-handle loops for Datadog, PagerDuty, Grafana, GitHub, and GitLab.
000539 | - Shared interface-driven parallel polling for AWS/GCP and other connectors with `poll_state + get_stats`.
000540 | [blank]
000541 | Each new event can go to OS desktop notification, console, and configured team channels. Desktop notification failures are intentionally non-fatal. Channels are Slack webhook, Discord webhook, SMTP email, and Twilio WhatsApp in `notifications.py`; incident-specific rich email and Slack Block Kit paths live separately.
000542 | [blank]
000543 | ### 9.2 Server watcher
000544 | [blank]
000545 | The FastAPI server has a distinct in-process watcher implementation around connector `WatchHandle`s and a one-second scheduler. It persists active watch metadata to YAML but stores actual handle objects and failure counters in memory. It creates notification records and WebSocket payloads; it does not reuse the CLI watcher’s dedup model in a single shared state object.
000546 | [blank]
000547 | ### 9.3 Duplicate/overlapping models
000548 | [blank]
000549 | There are at least four watcher/event consumers in the desktop and two watcher implementations in Python. This is functional but increases the chance of duplicate polls, duplicate sockets, inconsistent deduplication, and inconsistent status semantics.

000553 | ## 10. Incidents, chat sessions, email, and Slack
000554 | [blank]
000555 | ### 10.1 Incident state
000556 | [blank]
000557 | `incident_manager.py` loads/saves `.prash/incidents/incidents.json` and keeps `_INCIDENTS` in memory. An incident record includes:
000558 | [blank]
000559 | ```text
000560 | incident_id, title, service, namespace, severity, status,
000561 | resolution_status, cluster, tags, error_summary, diagnosis,
000562 | proposed_remediation, patch_data, agent_thinking, requires_approval,
000563 | episodic_memory, created/resolved timestamps, conversation[]
000564 | ```
000565 | [blank]
000566 | The lifecycle is ACTIVE/INVESTIGATING → RESOLVED/RECOVERED after `kubectl` remediation, or DENIED/ESCALATED_TO_HUMAN after denial. `approve_incident()` records the approver and immediately invokes `execute_remediation()`; `deny_incident()` changes state and appends conversation messages.
000567 | [blank]
000568 | The remediation subprocess currently patches a service ConfigMap, optionally scales a PostgreSQL deployment, deletes matching service pods, and then records a success message claiming health verification. The shown code does not itself perform the stated HTTP health probe before setting RESOLVED; this is a confirmed honesty/verification gap.
000569 | [blank]
000570 | ### 10.2 Chat session state
000571 | [blank]
000572 | `chat_manager.py` persists:
000573 | [blank]
000574 | - `.prash/chat_sessions/sessions_index.json`
000575 | - `.prash/chat_sessions/session_{id}.json`
000576 | [blank]
000577 | Sessions contain origin, service, incident linkage, status, timestamps, messages, and attachments. Channel session reuse is based on origin and recent activity; sender identity is recorded in message text/metadata but session lookup does not strictly key by sender.
000578 | [blank]
000579 | ### 10.3 Email
000580 | [blank]
000581 | `email_service.py` generates escaped HTML incident and Copilot emails, archives `.prash/emails/latest.html` and per-incident HTML, attempts SMTP, and records in-memory dispatched email metadata. It embeds localhost chat/approval URLs by default and has default recipient/sender fallbacks in source. `conversation_router.py` runs an IMAP Gmail listener in a daemon thread, processes up to the last five unseen messages, authorizes by configured sender/incident subject heuristics, and routes replies.
000582 | [blank]
000583 | ### 10.4 Slack
000584 | [blank]
000585 | `slack_service.py` emits Block Kit/webhook messages with war-room, approve, and deny URLs. `conversation_router.py` routes Slack commands/events/interactivity to channel-isolated sessions and responses. Slack status/commands are exposed through unauthenticated server routes; the actual webhook URLs are local credentials.
000586 | [blank]
000587 | ### 10.5 Demo-specific fixed narrative
000588 | [blank]
000589 | `conversation_router.py` contains a large triage-report generator with fixed host names, CPU/memory/latency values, service names, EKS details, and a 98.4% health score. `server.py`, `email_service.py`, `incident_manager.py`, and Slack code also contain default `checkout-api`/`lear-demo`/`ap-south-1` assumptions. These are appropriate for a demo path only, but several are reachable from shared Copilot/channel infrastructure and conflict with “all data dynamic” claims.

000592 | [blank]
000593 | ## 11. Persistence, configuration, and database/storage behavior
000594 | [blank]
000595 | ### 11.1 No database
000596 | [blank]
000597 | There is no SQL schema, migration, ORM model, database client, or database file used as the application’s persistence layer. The only database-like behaviors are:
000598 | [blank]
000599 | - demo incident names and a demo “database failure/failover” narrative;
000600 | - provider APIs such as CloudWatch/Datadog/PagerDuty;
000601 | - external Kubernetes/Cloud/Terraform state.
000602 | [blank]
000603 | ### 11.2 Local stores
000604 | [blank]
000605 | | Store | Default path | Owner/use | Lifetime/notes |
000606 | |---|---|---|---|
000607 | | Credentials | root `.env` for FastAPI; `.env` or `~/.prash/.env` for `CredentialStore` | connector keys, model keys, notification secrets, behavior settings | ignored; connect validates before atomic rewrite; CLI may append secrets |
000608 | | Project/watch/config YAML | root `prash.yaml` | projects, environments, services, active watches, settings, widget layouts | currently tracked in this checkout despite ignore rule; rewritten with `yaml.safe_dump` |
000609 | | Action audit | `.prash/audit.log` or `PRASH_AUDIT_LOG_PATH` | append-only JSONL actions/results | local, sequence scans file from end; no retention enforcement |
000610 | | Circuit breaker | `.prash/circuit.json` or `PRASH_CIRCUIT_STATE_PATH` | resource → recent action timestamps | local persisted safety cap |
000611 | | Episodic memory | `.prash/memory.json` or `PRASH_MEMORY_PATH` | verified fixes/signatures/outcomes | local JSON; malformed/missing store degrades empty |
000612 | | Notifications | `.prash/notifications.json` | max 100 notifications/read state | loaded at server lifespan; persisted on updates |
000613 | | Incidents | `.prash/incidents/incidents.json` | incident records/conversation | module creates directory on import; in-memory cache reloads from disk |
000614 | | Chat | `.prash/chat_sessions/sessions_index.json` + `session_*.json` | session index and full conversations | module creates directory on import; JSON rewrite per message |
000615 | | Email previews | `.prash/emails/latest.html`, `{incident}.html` | rendered incident/Copilot email | module creates directory; in-memory dispatch list capped separately |
000616 | | Browser selection | localStorage keys `lear_active_project_id`, `lear_active_environment` | active project/environment | browser-local, not shared with backend |
000617 | | Server process state | Python globals | watches, handles, clients, activity, connections, caches | lost on process restart except selected YAML/JSON stores |
000618 | [blank]
000619 | ### 11.3 Configuration key families
000620 | [blank]
000621 | - Models: `DEEPSEEK_API_KEY/MODEL/BASE_URL`, `KIMI_API_KEY/MODEL/BASE_URL`, `GEMINI_API_KEY`, `PRIMARY_MODEL`.
000622 | - Cloud: AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, Vercel keys.
000623 | - CI/observability/security: GitHub, GitLab, Datadog, Grafana, PagerDuty, Snyk, Gitleaks, Terraform.
000624 | - Safety: `PRASH_PERMISSION_MODE`, `PRASH_ENVIRONMENT`, circuit settings, audit path, max diagnosis concurrency.
000625 | - Watcher: interval and provider target lists.
000626 | - Channels: Slack/Discord webhooks, SMTP, Twilio/WhatsApp.
000627 | - Desktop settings: poll interval, retention, desktop notifications, degraded alerts.
000628 | [blank]
000629 | ### 11.4 Persistence risks
000630 | [blank]
000631 | - `prash.yaml` contains project/watch/layout/settings state and is broadly rewritten by unrelated features; concurrent writers are not centrally serialized.
000632 | - Incidents/chat JSON files are read-modify-written without a cross-process lock.
000633 | - Runtime global state is not an `AppState` object and is not consistently protected for concurrent request/thread access.
000634 | - `.prash` is ignored, but directories are eagerly created by imports, so merely importing certain modules mutates the working directory.
000635 | - `retention_days` is stored/read as a setting but no broad retention cleanup behavior was found in the core stores.
000636 | [blank]
000637 | ---
000638 | [blank]
000639 | ## 12. Infrastructure, packaging, and verification
000640 | [blank]
000641 | ### 12.1 Packaging
000642 | [blank]
000643 | `pyproject.toml` requires Python >=3.10 and declares Rich, Kubernetes, Pydantic, HTTPX, OpenAI, Plyer, Textual, boto3, Google auth/API clients, FastAPI/Uvicorn, dotenv, and PyYAML. Optional `desktop` and `dev` extras cover FastAPI server and pytest.
000644 | [blank]
000645 | The frontend package uses React 19, React Router 7, Radix UI, Framer Motion, Lucide, Vite 7, TypeScript 5.8, Vitest 5, React Testing Library, Tailwind/PostCSS, and Tauri 2 packages.
000646 | [blank]
000647 | ### 12.2 CI
000648 | [blank]
000649 | The Python CI runs on Ubuntu, Windows, and macOS, installs `.[dev]`, runs Ruff non-blocking, then pytest. Separate jobs run kind-based Kubernetes live tests and a Docker WireMock Grafana integration. The intentionally broken fixture runs only on branch `prash-broken-ci`.
000650 | [blank]
000651 | ### 12.3 Tauri limitations
000652 | [blank]
000653 | The Rust shell currently only provides `greet`. Tauri configuration has `csp: null`, opens `localhost:1420`, and includes only default core/opener permissions. Backend process supervision is done by external Windows scripts, not the Tauri shell.
000654 | [blank]
000655 | ### 12.4 Safe validation performed
000656 | [blank]
000657 | - `python -m compileall -q prash evals scripts tests` — **passed**.
000658 | - `pytest -q` — **not run successfully**; `pytest` is not installed in the audit environment (`/bin/bash: pytest: command not found`).
000659 | - Frontend build/tests — **not run**; `desktop/node_modules` is absent. No dependency installation was performed.
000660 | - No live cloud/Kubernetes/SMTP/IMAP/Slack/Twilio/model validation was attempted.
000661 | - No server was started and no external side effects were triggered.
000662 | [blank]

000664 | [blank]
000665 | ## 13. Confirmed discrepancy, risk, and unfinished-work register
000666 | [blank]
000667 | ### 13.1 Confirmed implementation issues
000668 | [blank]
000669 | 1. **Frontend configured-count contract mismatch.** `LearContext` filters `/api/connectors` results by `c.configured`; `registry_to_json()` returns `status: configured/unconfigured` and does not add a boolean `configured`. `Integrations.tsx` correctly checks `status`, but context-level `connectedCount` can be wrong.
000670 | 2. **Permissive CORS.** FastAPI uses wildcard origins with credentials.
000671 | 3. **Unauthenticated WebSocket.** `/ws/events` accepts any connection and controls pause/resume/stop by watch ID.
000672 | 4. **Unauthenticated incident mutation.** Approval/denial routes accept GET and POST and directly mutate/execute remediation.
000673 | 5. **Settings secret response.** `get_settings()` returns configured Slack/Discord/PagerDuty values through its settings payload rather than the registry’s masking helper.
000674 | 6. **Loopback-only runtime assumptions.** Root scripts, Vite proxy, WebSocket hook, email links, Slack links, and server `__main__` use localhost/127.0.0.1. This is unsuitable for a proxied browser/live preview without a relative/proxy-aware WebSocket and host binding.
000675 | 7. **Multiple WebSocket connections.** Context, notifications, watcher, and service widgets each create independent sockets.
000676 | 8. **Project delete watch cleanup is mismatched.** Project deletion looks for watch IDs beginning with `project_id`, while server watch IDs are `{connector}:{target}`; project deletion therefore does not reliably stop related watches.
000677 | 9. **Incident “verified” claims exceed shown verification.** `execute_remediation()` sets RESOLVED and records HTTP 200/1-of-1 language after subprocess patch/delete operations, without a visible health probe in that function.
000678 | 10. **Chat action execution is a high-privilege endpoint.** It parses model/user-provided argv and invokes CLI functions in-process; the endpoint substitutes an always-approve ask implementation for the request.
000679 | 11. **Hardcoded/demo narrative crosses shared paths.** Triage reports, Copilot prompts/fallbacks, incident defaults, and channel HTML contain fixed infrastructure names/metrics/URLs.
000680 | 12. **Resource discovery is incomplete by provider.** Registry has 13 connectors, but server resource discovery has explicit cases for only a subset.
000681 | 13. **Status detail field mismatch.** Project status uses `ResourceState.message`, while the base dataclass exposes `detail`; user-facing detail can be empty.
000682 | 14. **Optional-only connector configured semantics.** `is_connector_configured()` requires any env key for Gitleaks/Terraform/Kubernetes optional-only schemas; a documented executable-on-PATH/default-only setup can appear unconfigured.
000683 | 15. **Dashboard/UI text remains partly hardcoded.** Dynamic connector counts coexist with provider-specific fixed summaries and status language.
000684 | [blank]
000685 | ### 13.2 Security and production work explicitly still planned
000686 | [blank]
000687 | The Week 1 roadmap lists these as not started: typed Pydantic request models for all bodies/queries, rate limiting, CORS lockdown, credential expiry, full secrets audit/pre-commit, security headers, WebSocket authentication, server/CLI decomposition, shared state extraction, API versioning, UI token/library work, test coverage baseline, endpoint contract tests, and broader frontend tests.
000688 | [blank]
000689 | These are not assumptions about missing code; they are explicitly listed in `tasks/week1/README.md` and `ROADMAP.md` as future work.
000690 | [blank]
000691 | ### 13.3 Documentation/spec drift
000692 | [blank]
000693 | - `LEAR_HANDOFF.md` and desktop task specs describe many features as completed, while `ROADMAP.md` lists a production-hardening layer as not started.
000694 | - `diagnosis_agent.py`’s module documentation describes a CI-only/unchanged brain even though runtime/monitoring schema/context code is present.
000695 | - README, `.env.example`, registry metadata, and current provider/action registration have some stale labels (for example older “AWS read-only” wording adjacent to execute support).
000696 | - Root and desktop package/build conventions are split between browser/Tauri development and loopback-only launcher behavior.
000697 | [blank]

000703 | [blank]
000704 | 1. **What change is wanted?** For example: a bug fix, security hardening, new connector/action, UI redesign, deployment/preview support, database/storage redesign, or behavior change.
000705 | 2. **What is the desired scope?** One file, one feature, a production-hardening tranche, or an end-to-end redesign.
000706 | 3. **What must remain unchanged?** Local-first credential posture, existing API compatibility, demo surfaces, CLI behavior, action safety semantics, or current UI design.
000707 | 4. **What are the acceptance criteria?** Expected API/UI behavior, tests, security constraints, migration/backward-compatibility needs, and whether live-provider validation is allowed.
000708 | 5. **What should happen next?** Implement directly on this fixed branch, produce a plan first, add tests first, or open a review/PR after implementation.

001156 | ## 16. Deep line-level system-design context
001157 | [blank]
001158 | The owner requested a second completeness pass so a future implementation agent can understand the system before changing it. The companion artifact [`LEAR_FULL_SYSTEM_CONTEXT.md`](./LEAR_FULL_SYSTEM_CONTEXT.md) is the exhaustive source map for that purpose.
001159 | [blank]
001160 | This pass is deliberately more mechanical than the narrative audit:
001161 | [blank]
001162 | - It enumerates every tracked file in the checkout, including documentation, specifications, tests, fixtures, scripts, infrastructure, lockfiles, desktop assets, and the audit artifacts.
001163 | - For every UTF-8 text file it records byte size, SHA-256, total line count, structural symbols with exact start/end line ranges, detected routes/hooks/actions/network/process/persistence markers, and then emits every source line with its original 1-based line number.
001164 | - For binary files it records the path, byte size, SHA-256, and binary classification instead of inventing semantic source details.
001165 | - It distinguishes implementation, test, fixture, task/specification, documentation, configuration, generated-lock, script, infrastructure, and asset areas so future changes can be scoped against both code and the intended contract.
001166 | - Credential-looking fixture values are redacted in the companion context while key names, control flow, tests, and file/line locations remain visible. No live credential or provider call was used.
001167 | [blank]
001168 | The line-level context is not a substitute for the repository itself: before any change, the implementation agent must still re-open the exact current source lines and re-check the working tree. The context is a navigation and completeness contract, not permission to assume that prose, task status, or tests are correct.
001169 | [blank]
001170 | ### Completeness status
001171 | [blank]
001172 | - Product implementation was not changed by this audit.
001173 | - The context generator scans the current tracked-file set and reports its own excluded self-reference explicitly; the final tracked-file count is recorded in the context header.
001174 | - Any future code change invalidates the affected line ranges and hashes; regenerate the context after such a change.

000001 | # Lear Repository Audit Superprompt
000002 | [blank]
000003 | You are auditing the Lear / Prash repository at `/home/user/Lear-Avi-tasks` on the fixed branch `arena/01a0e95c-lear-avi-tasks`. The audit date is 2026-09-28 UTC. Do not change application behavior while auditing. Do not install dependencies, contact external providers, mutate cloud resources, send notifications, or create credentials. Work from the repository as the source of truth.
000004 | [blank]
000005 | ## Mission
000006 | [blank]
000007 | Build a source-grounded, end-to-end model of the entire application before proposing or implementing any change. Understand not only what the code is intended to do, but what it actually does at runtime, where state lives, what crosses trust boundaries, which paths are dynamic versus demo/hardcoded, and where documentation, tests, and implementation disagree.
000008 | [blank]
000009 | ## Required audit method
000010 | [blank]
000011 | 1. Inventory every tracked file and group it into product code, desktop code, Tauri shell, connectors, actions, AI/brain, watcher, persistence/configuration, tests, fixtures, evaluation harness, scripts, infrastructure, CI, and documentation.
000012 | 2. Perform a structural pass over all Python and TypeScript/Rust source: module imports, classes, functions, route decorators, action registrations, connector registry entries, persistence paths, environment variables, subprocess/network calls, and test coverage targets.
000013 | 3. Read deeply enough to trace every important execution path rather than stopping at filenames or docstrings. For each claimed behavior, identify its implementation source and caller/callee chain.
000014 | 4. Trace the main user journeys end to end:
000015 |    - first launch and onboarding;
000016 |    - connector connect, validate, status, disconnect, and credential persistence;
000017 |    - project/environment/service creation and health polling;
000018 |    - dashboard metrics, generated widgets, activity, notifications;
000019 |    - watch start, restore, poll, pause/resume, stop, WebSocket broadcast, and notifications;
000020 |    - chat intent resolution, telemetry injection, streaming, approval, command execution, and audit;
000021 |    - CLI investigate/fix/run/watch/repl/TUI flows;
000022 |    - diagnosis, log acquisition, schema validation, memory, correlation, multi-failure diagnosis, remediation, verification, and reconciliation;
000023 |    - incidents and approval through dashboard, war room, email, and Slack;
000024 |    - demo/storefront/admin surfaces.
000025 | 5. Map every connector through the shared contract: auth inputs, real provider APIs or local subprocesses, locate/poll/log/stats/watch behavior, write capabilities, normalization, error handling, and action mappings.
000026 | 6. Map every write action through `plan -> circuit breaker -> permission decision -> approval/secret handling -> execute -> verify -> breaker record -> audit`. Record the action ID, risk tier, reversibility, target, and external side effects.
000027 | 7. Map every state store and data lifetime. Distinguish process memory, localStorage, YAML, dotenv, JSON, append-only logs, generated HTML, model-provider state, and external-provider state. Record exact paths, schemas, load/save timing, retention limits, and concurrency/atomicity behavior.
000028 | 8. Audit trust and safety boundaries: secret masking, credential persistence, raw request bodies, shell commands, subprocess use, SMTP/IMAP/webhooks, CORS, WebSocket auth, URL construction, HTML escaping, approval routes, audit completeness, circuit-breaker scope, and demo code.
000029 | 9. Compare implementation against README, handoff, roadmap, task specs, changelog, CI, and tests. Mark each discrepancy as implemented, partially implemented, planned, stale, demo-only, or unverified.
000030 | 10. Run only safe local validation available in the environment. At minimum run Python compilation and inspect git status. If tests/builds cannot run because dependencies are absent, record that precisely; do not silently install dependencies or use live credentials.
000031 | [blank]
000032 | ## Evidence rules
000033 | [blank]
000034 | - Prefer exact file paths, symbols, route names, environment keys, and observed code behavior over marketing language.
000035 | - Never call a value “live” merely because a UI label says live. Distinguish provider API data, local fixture data, generated fallback data, and hardcoded demo narrative.
000036 | - Never assume a database exists. Prove whether SQL/ORM/database files are present and describe the actual persistence layer.
000037 | - Treat secrets as toxic data. Do not print, copy, or persist credential values in the audit artifact. Report only key names, masking behavior, and exposure risks.
000038 | - Treat an action that can mutate infrastructure as potentially dangerous even if its UI label says “safe.” Record whether approval is enforced at every ingress path.
000039 | - Call out stale comments and documentation when they materially misdescribe the current implementation.
000040 | - Call out duplicate state, race-prone globals, endpoint contract mismatches, hardcoded provider assumptions, missing authentication, and unavailable test coverage.
000041 | [blank]
000042 | ## Deliverable format
000043 | [blank]
000044 | Produce:
000045 | [blank]
000046 | 1. A concise executive architecture map.
000047 | 2. A complete file inventory with categories and counts.
000048 | 3. A detailed runtime and data-flow map for backend, desktop, CLI, connectors, actions, brain, watcher, incidents, notifications, and persistence.
000049 | 4. A connector and action capability matrix.
000050 | 5. A storage/configuration/database statement with exact paths and schemas.
000051 | 6. A UI/surface map describing what a user sees and how navigation/state changes.
000052 | 7. A test/build/verification report with commands and exact limitations.
000053 | 8. An evidence-based discrepancy, risk, and unfinished-work register. Separate confirmed defects from roadmap work and unverified hypotheses.
000054 | 9. A reusable list of questions for the owner: what change is wanted, desired scope, safety constraints, acceptance criteria, and what to do next.
000055 | [blank]
000056 | Do not implement a product change until the owner answers the final questions. Keep the audit itself non-invasive and leave the working tree clean except for explicitly requested audit artifacts.
````

This is a stronger notify-not-gate, not a notify-and-gate.

000060 | [blank]
000061 | ## 1. Why we're pivoting (context for anyone reading this cold)
000062 | [blank]
000063 | Prash v1 is a hosted service: it watches GitHub Actions, diagnoses why a CI run failed, and opens a pull request with a fix. It works, and it's live at prash.drufiy.com.
000064 | [blank]
000065 | We ran it against 13 real CI failures across 9 real open-source repos — not synthetic tests, actual broken builds on other people's projects. The result reframed the product:
000066 | [blank]
000067 | **Only ~5 of 13 failures were fixable by editing a file.** The other 8 needed something Prash structurally couldn't do: add a secret, fix a permission, know a value a security scanner deliberately redacted, decide whether a stale submodule URL should be updated or the repo made public. Prash can only write diffs. It has no way to *act*.
000068 | [blank]
000069 | This isn't a bug. It's the ceiling of the product as designed. No better prompt or model closes it, because the problem isn't diagnosis quality — it's that ~60% of real-world CI failures require doing something outside a code diff.
000070 | [blank]
000071 | **The deeper finding:** an AI agent creates value when the *machine has more context than the human it's helping*. CI repair is structurally the worst possible place to test that, because the person who broke the build 30 seconds ago already knows more than any model can reconstruct. The places where the asymmetry flips — production incidents at 3am, Kubernetes failures with no obvious cause, a system nobody has fully in their head — are where an agent is actually worth something.
000072 | [blank]
000073 | **The decision:** stop trying to perfect CI repair in isolation. Build Prash into a general-purpose AI DevOps agent — something that watches infrastructure the way Claude Code watches a codebase, and can *act* on what it finds, not just describe it.
000074 | [blank]
000075 | ---
000076 | [blank]
000077 | ## 2. What Lear actually is, in one paragraph
000078 | [blank]
000079 | **Sharpened 2026-08-18 — team positioning decision, full reasoning in §9.** Prash is an AI DevOps agent with two modes on one shared brain, one local credential store, and one audit log. In **autopilot** — the hero mode — Prash runs continuously in the environment a team gives it access to (CI, cloud, Kubernetes, deployments), the way an on-call engineer would, except it never sleeps: the moment something looks wrong it notifies the team over their own channel (Slack, Discord, email — whatever's configured), then acts within whatever permission tier it's been trusted with — safe fixes on its own, anything riskier only with a human's yes. In **copilot** mode, an engineer drops into the local CLI + REPL to drive Prash directly — deep-diving an incident, brainstorming the fix together, watching it land — deliberately the same interaction shape as Claude Code, for familiarity. Same credentials, same audit trail, either way: they stay local, under the team's control, and Drufiy's servers never hold them. Built first for **startups and small tech companies**, where the engineers *are* the on-call rotation and the pain is sharpest — not an enterprise sale that needs a security review before it can prove itself.
000080 | [blank]
000081 | *Original 2026-08-03 framing, kept for the record, not the current pitch: "Prash becomes a local agent, in the shape of Claude Code, that a developer or ops engineer installs and points at their own infrastructure..." — see git history for the full original paragraph.*
000082 | [blank]
000083 | ---
000084 | [blank]
000085 | ## 3. The workflow — concretely, step by step
000086 | [blank]
000087 | **Install & connect (once).**
000088 | The user installs Prash locally (CLI, npm/pip package, or eventually a desktop app). They point it at a local `.env`-style file holding their own credentials — GCP key, Kubernetes context, Vercel token, whatever they want it watching. Nothing is uploaded to Drufiy at this step. This is exactly the model Claude Code itself uses for API keys.
000089 | [blank]
000090 | **Background watching.**
000091 | Once configured, a lightweight Prash process runs continuously — on the user's machine, or on a server they control — polling the systems it has access to: CI status, pod health, deploy state, error rates. This is the "always on" half of the product that a request/response CLI alone can't provide.
000092 | [blank]
000093 | **Something breaks.**
000094 | Prash notices — a pod is crash-looping, a deploy failed, a CI run broke. It pings the user (desktop notification, Slack, whatever channel is configured). It does **not** silently act on anything above the "safe" tier without this step.
000095 | [blank]
000096 | **The user opens the Prash interface.**
000097 | This is the working surface — modeled on Claude Code's own interaction pattern, not a static dashboard. Prash presents:
000098 | - what it found and why it thinks that's the cause
000099 | - what it wants to do about it
000100 | - for safe actions: it just does them, and shows what it did
000101 | - for anything riskier: it asks first, in plain language, before touching anything
000102 | [blank]
000103 | **Verification.**
000104 | After any action, Prash checks whether it actually worked — re-checks the pod, re-runs the check, confirms the metric recovered — and reports back honestly if it didn't, rather than claiming success it can't verify.
000105 | [blank]
000106 | **v1 interface scope:** a rich CLI/terminal interface (matching Claude Code's actual current form factor) ships this sprint. A full desktop app is a later phase, not part of the two-week build — don't scope it in now.
000107 | [blank]
000108 | ---
000109 | [blank]
000110 | ## 4. Architecture — the part that determines whether anyone trusts this
000111 | [blank]
000112 | ### The decision: credentials never leave the user's machine
000113 | [blank]
000114 | We explicitly rejected Prash's servers holding user cloud/Kubernetes/deploy credentials directly. Reasoning:
000115 | [blank]
000116 | - If Drufiy's servers held live AWS keys, kubectl access, and registry credentials for every customer, a breach of *our* infrastructure becomes a breach of *every customer's production environment simultaneously*. That's a fundamentally different risk class than the GitHub App token Prash v1 already holds (scoped to opening PRs, revocable by GitHub, bounded blast radius).
000117 | - Real engineering orgs run long security reviews before granting that kind of access to any third party. For a small team, that access model is close to unsellable to anyone with an actual security function, and a genuine liability if we're ever compromised.
000118 | - The alternative costs us nothing to build — it's an absence of infrastructure, not a feature. "Your keys never touch our servers" is a stronger trust claim than any encryption story, and Claude Code's own adoption is the existence proof that developers accept this model without friction.
000119 | [blank]
000120 | **So:** credentials live in a local file, under the user's control, always. Drufiy's servers never receive them, never store them, never see them in transit for the purpose of *acting* on infrastructure.
000121 | [blank]
000122 | ### What's hosted vs. what's local
000123 | [blank]
000124 | | | Runs where | Holds credentials? |
000125 | |---|---|---|
000126 | | The watcher (polls CI, cloud, k8s, deploys) | User's machine or their own server | No — reads local `.env` only |
000127 | | The action engine (diagnose, fix, restart, roll back) | User's machine or their own server | No — uses local credentials directly |
000128 | | The interface (what the user opens when pinged) | Local (CLI/terminal this sprint) | No |
000129 | | Notifications, cross-project history, team visibility | Can be hosted (Drufiy-run) | No — status and audit-log data only, never secrets |
000130 | | Prash v1's existing GitHub webhook service | Stays exactly as-is, untouched | GitHub App token only (existing, scoped, already how it works today) |
000131 | [blank]
000132 | The existing hosted service (prash.drufiy.com, repo `Drufiy/prash-backend`) is **not being rebuilt or retired.** It keeps watching GitHub the way it does today. This repo (`prash-v2-backend`) is new and separate — not a fork, not a branch.
000133 | [blank]
000134 | ### What carries over from v1 (verified by inspection, not assumed)
000135 | [blank]
000136 | We checked how tightly each part of the v1 codebase depends on the hosted database/web stack:
000137 | [blank]
000138 | | Module (in `prash-backend`) | Depends on hosted stack? | Verdict |
000139 | |---|---|---|
000140 | | `diagnosis_agent.py` — prompts, guardrails, confidence logic, honest-refusal behavior (~1,200 lines) | **Zero** | Port to this repo unchanged |
000141 | | `log_fetcher.py` — log parsing, error filtering, per-job budgeting | **Zero** | Port unchanged |
000142 | | `schemas.py`, `repo_memory.py` | Zero | Port unchanged |
000143 | | `kimi_client.py` (model calling) | 3 minor spots (optional call-logging) | Port after a trivial fix |
000144 | | `processor.py` (orchestration) | Heavy (22 couplings) | Does not port — this repo gets its own orchestrator |
000145 | | `webhook.py`, `reconciler.py`, hosted routes | Heavy | Stay in `prash-backend`, untouched |
000146 | [blank]
000147 | **The valuable IP — the actual diagnosis intelligence — has zero ties to the web stack and moves across as-is.** We are not starting over. We're keeping the brain and giving it a new body. This porting work is **Track D**, owned by Aradhya — see §6.
000148 | [blank]
000149 | Also directly reusable from `prash-backend`: `vercel_client.py` as the template for every new connector (authenticate → locate resource → fetch logs → poll state), `deploy_repair.py` as existing proof the loop already works on non-CI failures, and the `evals/` harness for measuring whether changes actually help.
000150 | [blank]
000151 | ---
000152 | [blank]
000153 | ## 5. What Prash is allowed to do — the inclusion rule
000154 | [blank]
000155 | "Eventually it does everything" is how scope dies. The rule for whether an action gets built:
000156 | [blank]
000157 | > An action ships when it is **(1) needed often**, **(2) verifiable** — we can check afterward whether it worked — and **(3) reversible or low-risk**. Anything that fails (3) always requires explicit approval, regardless of permission mode, including any "bypass" automation mode.
000158 | [blank]
000159 | ### v1 capability set
000160 | [blank]
000161 | **Read / investigate (no permission needed):**
000162 | GitHub Actions logs, Vercel build logs, Cloud Run logs, Kubernetes pod status/logs/events.
000163 | [blank]
000164 | **Act — safe tier (can run without asking, in permissive modes):**
000165 | Re-run a failed job. Restart a crash-looping pod or service. Open a fix PR. Ask the user for a missing secret.
000166 | [blank]
000167 | **Act — approval tier (always asks, even in bypass mode):**
000168 | Roll back a deployment. Scale resources up/down. Apply a config change.
000169 | [blank]
000170 | **Never, in v1:**
000171 | Database migrations. Anything that destroys data. Anything touching production without an explicit, per-action grant.
000172 | [blank]
000173 | ### Permission modes (mirrors Claude Code's own model)
000174 | [blank]
000175 | `read-only` → `ask every time` (default) → `auto-safe` (safe tier proceeds automatically, approval tier still prompts) → `environment-scoped` (auto on staging, always prompts on production) → `bypass` (for CI/automation use; still refuses the "never" list unconditionally).
000176 | [blank]
000177 | **Status: this is already substantially built.** Aryan's local (unpushed as of 2026-08-09) work has all five modes implemented with passing tests covering exactly this matrix — see §9 decision log and §10 item from 2026-08-09.
000178 | [blank]

Before adding any new platform from §7b, the product gets hardened: both founders use it for real on their own machines, the interface becomes genuinely interactive, and bugs found by real use get fixed. **Timebox: 2-3 days.** Nothing from §7b's expansion list starts until this phase's exit criteria are met.
000277 | [blank]
000278 | ### Why this phase exists (and what triggered it)
000279 | [blank]
000280 | Aradhya installed and ran Prash as an actual user — not as its author — for the first time on 2026-08-14. Two things surfaced immediately that no amount of test-writing had caught:
000281 | 1. **A blank `.env` value broke the whole thing out of the box** (§10) — `KUBECONFIG=` left empty, exactly as `.env.example` instructs, exported as an empty string and made the Kubernetes client fail. 138 passing tests didn't catch it because no test ever ran the real first-run setup path.
000282 | 2. **There is no interactive interface.** Prash is a set of discrete argument-based commands. The stated product bar — an agent you talk to, that feels like magic — is not what's built. That gap was a deliberate sprint-1 scope cut (§7), but it's now the top priority.
000283 | [blank]
000284 | The lesson, consistent with §1's whole thesis: **real use finds things tests structurally cannot.** This phase is that, deliberately, for 2-3 days.
